Ea-Nasir was a merchant from the city of Ur in ancient Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq) during the early 2nd millennium BCE. He is known from a collection of letters written to him by a man named Shipti-Ishar, who was a high-ranking official in the court of King Shulgi of Ur. These letters, known as the "Ur Letters," provide valuable insights into the economic and social conditions of the time.

Ea-Nasir was a successful businessman who dealt in various commodities such as copper, tin, and textiles. He had a significant amount of wealth and influence, as indicated by his correspondence with Shipti-Ishar. The letters discuss business transactions, personal matters, and even legal disputes, offering a glimpse into the daily life and commerce of the ancient Near East.

One of the most famous aspects of Ea-Nasir's story is his refusal to provide a loan to Shipti-Ishar, despite their long-standing business relationship. This refusal is documented in one of the letters and has been the subject of scholarly debate regarding the nature of their relationship and the reasons behind Ea-Nasir's decision.

The "Ur Letters" are an important source of information for historians and archaeologists studying the ancient Near East, and Ea-Nasir's role in these letters has contributed to our understanding of the economic and social structures of the time.
